thesis.body: A dedicated decision model may be enough to route a research agent—without paying a general-purpose language model to make every routing decision. The test is whether Jev preserves answer quality while reducing total cost or active time.
thesis.why: Choosing the next action and writing the next piece of text are different jobs. Separating them lets the benchmark ask a narrower question: how much model do we need for the decision?
when: The decision is a choice among explicit actions, such as search, read, or answer.
The agent can provide structured state: evidence, unread results, history, and the remaining budget.
The complete agent can be evaluated against a language-model decider and a fixed baseline.
whenNot: The task is to generate an open-ended query, explanation, or final answer; those remain with the language model in this design.
A fixed sequence already solves the task well enough; the benchmark includes that baseline.
The only evidence is a cheaper routing call. Answer quality and whole-agent cost still need to hold up.
thesis.method: The v2 suite holds Claude Haiku 5.5 generation fixed and compares three decision-model controllers (Jev, MSFT, and OAI), three Claude deciders (Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus), and a fixed baseline. The 50-question dataset spans seven categories, including multi-hop research, recent facts, arithmetic, and unanswerable questions. Phoenix evaluates correctness, groundedness, routing fit, cost, and active latency.

learnings.title: Isolate the decision you are trying to measure.
learnings.body: The generator stays fixed while the decider changes. That makes the routing strategy the comparison, rather than changing the controller and the text-generation model together.

learnings.title: A research benchmark needs questions that require research.
learnings.body: The original preparation used a partial closed-book screen to avoid known answers. The v2 suite expands to 50 questions across seven categories, including recent facts, multi-entity research, arithmetic, multi-hop FRAMES, and unanswerable questions. This tests more than one kind of routing decision.

learnings.title: Correctness and evidence support are different checks.
learnings.body: The v2 evaluators grade the answer against accepted variants, distinguish a committed answer from a hedge, and separately check whether the collected notes support its key claim. Routing fit, cost, and active latency provide additional views of how the agent reached the outcome.

learnings.title: An evaluation is only useful if it belongs to the current output.
learnings.body: After a failed run is resumed, a grade from the failed attempt can remain attached to its run ID. The repair checks evaluation timestamps against the new run and backfills stale or missing evaluations.

challenges.title: The first full run was interrupted.
challenges.challenge: The original benchmark plan records a network outage while the machine slept, leaving failed or missing runs.
challenges.solution: The runner supports resuming failed or missing runs, then resuming evaluations. This avoids deliberately rerunning successful examples.

challenges.title: Distinct metrics collapsed into one evaluator column.
challenges.challenge: The code-based metric closures shared the same qualified function name, so Phoenix treated them as the same evaluator.
challenges.solution: Give each metric evaluator a unique name that Phoenix recognizes, and explicitly mark correctness as an LLM evaluator.

challenges.title: Resumed outputs inherited stale grades.
challenges.challenge: Reusing a run ID meant an earlier failed attempt could still carry an empty-prediction grade after the task succeeded.
challenges.solution: Compare evaluation and task timestamps, redo evaluations older than the current run, and upsert results by run and evaluator name.

challenges.title: Shared throttling distorted wall-clock comparisons.
challenges.challenge: Concurrent agents queue behind a per-model request limiter. That wait can obscure the time actually spent doing the task.
challenges.solution: Track queue wait per thread and report active latency separately from elapsed wall time.

takeaways.title: Use a decision model for a bounded decision.
takeaways.body: Define the available actions and the state the controller can inspect. Keep query writing, note taking, and answer generation with the language model in this architecture.

takeaways.title: Keep a simple baseline in the comparison.
takeaways.body: A fixed sequence establishes whether adaptive routing adds value at all. A more capable decider is useful only if the complete task benefits.

takeaways.title: Make the recommendation from complete, current evidence.
takeaways.body: Check correctness, evidence support, cost, and active latency together. Repair missing or stale grades before interpreting the comparison. The v2 suite and evaluators are implemented; a final performance analysis has not been loaded into this presentation, so these remain working implementation takeaways—not a claim that Jev wins.
